Name: conservation_invariance_probing
Title: Do Scientific Foundation Models Internally Conserve What Nature Conserves? Probing for Latent Invariants and Symmetry Structure
Short Hypothesis: Established science is organized around conserved quantities and symmetries (mass/atom balance in reactions, charge, energy, stoichiometry, chirality/parity, Noether-type invariances). We hypothesize that a foundation model which genuinely understands a domain encodes these conserved quantities as *invariant directions* in its representation space — i.e., representations move along a low-dimensional manifold under transformations that preserve the conserved quantity and move off-manifold under transformations that violate it — and that the degree to which a model's internal geometry respects each conservation law/symmetry is a measurable, read-only diagnostic that predicts where the model produces physically inconsistent outputs.
Related Work: Two adjacent lines exist. (1) Physics-informed models (CLOUD, Dynami-CAL GraphNet, conservation-informed GNNs) *architecturally enforce* conservation/symmetry as an inductive bias; they do not test whether an unconstrained foundation model *spontaneously* represents these invariants. (2) Output-level physical-plausibility evaluations (Morpheus for Newtonian video generation) score whether generated outputs obey conservation laws, but treat the model as a black box and never inspect internal representations. Sanz (2026) reviews how symmetries reduce latent dimensionality in VAEs for toy physics/particle data, but not for pretrained scientific foundation models nor as a per-law diagnostic. Our contribution is orthogonal and novel: a read-only, model-agnostic framework that measures whether *specific* scientific conservation laws and symmetries are encoded as representational invariances, distinguishes conservation-respecting from violation-sensitive transformations, and links internal invariance fidelity to downstream physical-consistency errors. It also differs from all four of my prior proposals (causal intervention, scaling-exponent recovery, cross-model universality, superseded-theory competition) by targeting invariance/symmetry structure rather than directional laws, exponents, cross-model agreement, or historical error.
Abstract: Much of established science is bookkeeping of conserved quantities and symmetries: chemical reactions conserve atoms and charge, physical processes conserve energy and momentum, molecules have chirality/parity structure, and crystals have space-group symmetry. Foundation models for chemistry, biology, and materials are not built to respect these constraints yet often make accurate predictions — raising the question of whether they internally represent conservation laws or merely approximate them. We introduce Conservation-Invariance Probing, a read-only framework that tests whether a conserved quantity is encoded as an invariant direction in a model's representation space. For each law, we construct paired input transformations that either *preserve* the conserved quantity (e.g., reordering reactants, relabeling equivalent atoms, applying a symmetry operation, balancing a reaction) or *violate* it (e.g., silently deleting an atom, breaking charge balance, mirroring a chiral center, changing stoichiometry). We measure representational movement under each: a model that understands the law should be near-invariant to preserving transforms and sensitive to violating transforms. We define a Conservation-Invariance Score aggregating (i) invariance to symmetry-preserving transforms, (ii) sensitivity to violations, and (iii) linear decodability of the conserved quantity. We validate the score by testing whether low-invariance laws predict the model's own physically inconsistent outputs (e.g., unbalanced reactions, symmetry-inconsistent property predictions). Applied to open molecular, protein, and materials models across ~10 laws, the framework yields a cheap, reproducible audit of which conservation principles a scientific model has truly internalized.
Experiments: 1. Law/symmetry curation (~10): chemistry — atom conservation (mass balance) in reactions, charge conservation, stoichiometric invariance, chirality/parity (R vs S enantiomers), reactant-permutation invariance in reaction SMILES; materials — crystal space-group symmetry operations, composition-normalization invariance, supercell equivalence; biology/proteins — sequence-frame/label permutation invariance for equivalent residues, disulfide-pairing charge/parity constraints. For each, define a *preserving* transform set and a *violating* transform set with matched surface-form magnitude. 2. Models: open molecular transformers (e.g., ChemBERTa/MolFormer), a materials encoder (e.g., a public crystal LM such as CLOUD-style or MatBERT), and ESM-2 (multiple sizes) for protein-side laws. 3. Representation extraction: for each input and its transformed variants, extract pooled and token-level representations at every layer. 4. Invariance measurement: compute representational displacement (normalized L2 / cosine) under preserving vs violating transforms; a conserved quantity is 'geometrically respected' when preserving displacement is small and violating displacement is large. Report per-layer invariance ratio = violating_displacement / preserving_displacement. 5. Conserved-quantity decodability: fit a linear probe to read the conserved quantity (e.g., total atom count, net charge, chirality label, space group) from representations; high decodability + high invariance ratio indicates genuine encoding. 6. Conservation-Invariance Score (CIS): combine (i) preserving-transform invariance, (ii) violation sensitivity (ideally with monotone response to violation magnitude, e.g., number of atoms deleted), and (iii) probe decodability, per law and layer. 7. Controls: random surface-form edits of matched magnitude (null for 'does the model just react to any change?'), randomly-initialized-model control, and shuffled-label probe null. 8. Downstream-validation: test whether laws with low CIS predict the model's own physically inconsistent predictions — e.g., for reaction models, rate of predicting products that violate atom/charge balance; for materials, rate of symmetry-inconsistent property predictions across equivalent inputs; for proteins, inconsistency of stability/property predictions under equivalent relabelings. Correlate per-law CIS with per-law downstream inconsistency rate (Spearman / AUROC of CIS distinguishing well- vs poorly-obeyed laws). 9. Scaling analysis: repeat across model sizes to test whether conservation fidelity emerges with scale. Metrics: invariance ratio, violation-magnitude monotonicity (Spearman), probe R^2/accuracy, CIS, and CIS-vs-downstream-inconsistency correlation. Deliverable: an open per-law Conservation-Invariance benchmark and leaderboard across public scientific models.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1. Preserving transforms may not be perfectly invariance-neutral for a given tokenization (e.g., SMILES canonicalization changes token strings), confounding 'law violation' with 'surface change'; we control with matched-magnitude random surface edits and use multiple equivalent surface forms to isolate semantic from lexical effects. 2. Conserved quantities may be encoded nonlinearly; we add nonlinear-probe robustness checks and treat linear results as a lower bound. 3. Constructing clean violation sets with graded magnitude is easier in chemistry/materials than in proteins; some protein laws may only support binary preserving/violating tests. 4. A model can be invariant to a transform for the wrong reason (insensitivity to all inputs); the decodability and violation-sensitivity components of CIS guard against trivially-invariant collapse. 5. The downstream-inconsistency link is correlational, not causal; we report it as validation evidence, not proof, and complement with per-law qualitative analysis. 6. Availability and comparability of open models differ across domains, which may restrict cross-model claims to within-domain comparisons — itself an informative scoping result.
